q1: Because the entity is still 'high-grade spindle cell/mesenchymal neoplasm, NOS,' there is no standard or proven chemotherapy, so I would make the decision explicitly empiric and prefer a clinical trial. If the family wants to start now, I would offer single-agent oral temozolomide (e.g., 150-200 mg/m2 on days 1-5 every 28 days) as the best-tolerated CNS-penetrant bridge while molecular and tissue results are pending. Other chemotherapy options that could be discussed if treating empirically as a high-grade soft-tissue/CNS sarcoma include a nitrosourea (lomustine/CCNU), anthracycline-based therapy (doxorubicin or liposomal doxorubicin +/- ifosfamide with mesna), single-agent ifosfamide, dacarbazine, trabectedin, gemcitabine/docetaxel, etoposide, or cyclophosphamide. These have greater toxicity and, for several agents, poor CNS penetration, and none is validated for this undefined entity, so I would not default to a multi-drug regimen. I would also pursue local control options for the growing resection margin (safe re-resection or focal re-irradiation if feasible), CSF assessment, and complete systemic staging, and I would not use an unconfirmed targeted agent. If the C6 nodule is confirmed as leptomeningeal disease, CNS-directed therapy/intrathecal chemotherapy would be considered with a specialist.
q2: I would not add a second chemotherapy drug at this point. The tumor remains unclassified, and there is no evidence that adding a second cytotoxic agent (for example lomustine/CCNU, etoposide, irinotecan, or an anthracycline) to temozolomide improves outcome in this entity; it would only add myelosuppression and other toxicity. The patient is tolerating single-agent temozolomide, which is serving as an empiric bridge, so I would continue it, monitor with imaging and blood counts, and await tissue/liquid-biopsy molecular results and a clinical trial option. If the entity is later defined as a high-grade sarcoma, an anthracycline +/- ifosfamide regimen could be considered; if defined as a high-grade glioma with MGMT promoter methylation, a temozolomide-based regimen (with or without lomustine in a trial) could be relevant. Bevacizumab is not a second chemotherapy drug and would be used only for symptomatic radiation necrosis/edema, not as empiric antitumor therapy.
q3: No. I would not stop temozolomide and switch to targeted therapy on the basis of this peripheral-blood ctDNA report alone. First, the final histologic entity is still undefined, and a molecular alteration does not by itself establish the diagnosis or prove that the alteration is the tumor driver. Second, plasma ctDNA in CNS tumors has limited sensitivity and specificity; a multi-alteration profile can reflect clonal hematopoiesis, a second/extracranial malignancy, or technical artifact, and discordance with the earlier tumor tissue panel must be resolved. The combination of FGFR2 fusion with KRAS, STK11, and CTNNB1 alterations in particular warrants evaluation for an occult non-CNS primary. Before changing therapy I would (1) confirm the FGFR2 fusion and the other alterations in tumor tissue with an RNA-based fusion assay/FISH and immunohistochemistry, using archived resection tissue or a repeat biopsy/resection of the growing margin; (2) complete systemic staging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or FDG-PET/CT) and CSF assessment; and (3) review at a molecular tumor board. If an FGFR2 fusion is confirmed in tissue and the tumor is shown to be FGFR-dependent, a CNS-penetrant FGFR inhibitor or an FGFR-directed trial could be considered and might replace chemotherapy. KRAS, STK11, and CTNNB1 are not currently directly actionable with standard agents in this setting unless a specific target such as KRAS G12C is confirmed. In the meantime, continue temozolomide if tolerated and the disease is not clearly progressing, and prioritize tissue confirmation and trial enrollment.
